papers.title: Identification and Validation of the ESR1 Y537S Mutant-Enriched Enhancer and Its Downstream Target IGFBP3
papers.authors: Amzaleg Y, Mecenas D, Flowers E, Li L, et al.

bibliographic.title: Identification and Validation of the ESR1 Y537S Mutant-Enriched Enhancer and Its Downstream Target IGFBP3

reading.one_line_takeaway: A 446 bp enhancer in the first intron of the pseudogene DPY19L1P1 on chromosome 7 is preferentially occupied by ESR1 Y537S mutant ERalpha and is required, in a mutant-specific way, for proliferation, adhesion, xenograft growth and fulvestrant resistance, acting at least in part by sustaining expression of IGFBP3.
reading.tldr: ESR1 ligand-binding-domain hotspot mutations such as Y537S make ERalpha constitutively active and are found in 18% to 53% of ER-positive breast cancers progressing on endocrine therapy, but it was not known whether the mutant-specific ER binding sites seen in ChIP-seq are functionally required. The authors performed ERalpha ChIP-seq in BRx68, a circulating tumor cell line carrying heterozygous ESR1 Y537S, intersected the peaks with three published MCF7 Y537S ChIP-seq datasets, and converged on a 446 bp region in the first intron of the pseudogene DPY19L1P1 (chr7:32,720,197 to 32,720,643) that carries enhancer chromatin marks, is more open in Y537S than wild-type MCF7 cells, contains a palindromic estrogen response element, and is bound more strongly by Y537S ER than by estrogen-activated wild-type ER. CRISPR deletion of this region impaired proliferation (days 3 and 7), collagen adhesion, anchorage-independent colony growth and mammary fat pad xenograft growth, and increased fulvestrant sensitivity, in Y537S cells only, with no comparable effect in wild-type cells. RNA-seq of the deletion clones crossed against Y537S-specific upregulated genes pointed to IGFBP3 and CD44, and IGFBP3 was higher in ESR1-mutant (n = 12) than wild-type (n = 34) ER-positive metastases in MET500. Knocking out IGFBP3 reduced day 7 proliferation in two of three clones but did not change fulvestrant sensitivity, so IGFBP3 accounts for part of the growth phenotype but not for the resistance phenotype.
reading.research_question: Do ESR1 ligand-binding-domain mutants drive endocrine resistance through mutant-specific cis-regulatory elements, and if so can one such enhancer be identified from ER ChIP-seq, shown to be functionally required in a mutation-dependent way, and connected to a downstream target gene?
reading.background: About 80% of breast cancers express ERalpha, and endocrine therapy that blocks or degrades ERalpha is the backbone of treatment, reducing recurrence by 50% and mortality by more than 25% in early-stage disease. Still, roughly 30% of patients are innately resistant and about 40% of initial responders acquire resistance. Exome sequencing of resistant metastases found recurrent ESR1 point mutations concentrated in the ligand-binding domain, present in 18% to 53% of patients progressing on endocrine therapy, with Y537S and D538G the two most common. These mutants behave like ligand-activated ERalpha without estrogen, and molecular dynamics modeling indicates reduced affinity for ER antagonists, which explains reduced fulvestrant effect in Y537S circulating tumor cells and in edited cell lines. Several groups had already shown that mutant ER has a transcriptome and a genome-wide binding landscape distinct from activated wild-type ER (refs 17 to 20), so candidate mutant-unique binding sites existed. The gap this paper fills is functional: none of those mutant-unique sites had been deleted and tested to see whether it is actually required for mutant-driven phenotypes, and none had been tied to a specific downstream gene.
reading.study_design: Discovery used ERalpha ChIP-seq in BRx68, an ER-positive circulating tumor cell line from a patient with luminal metastatic breast cancer carrying heterozygous ESR1 Y537S, grown in suspension at 10 million cells per 500 cm2 dish, with two biological replicates treated 24 hours with 10 nmol/L 17beta-estradiol or ethanol vehicle, using the Santa Cruz HC-20 ER antibody with IgG control and a 15 million read target. Peaks (MACS2, FDR < 0.05 versus sonicated input) were compared with MCF7 wild-type and Y537S peaks and with three published MCF7 Y537S ChIP-seq datasets (Jeselsohn ref 17, Harrod ref 19, Li ref 20). Chromatin context came from ENCODE histone data across seven cell lines, from ATAC-seq (50,000 cells per sample, Tn5 transposition, 10 million paired-end reads) in MCF7 wild-type, Y537S and D538G cells, and from H3K4me1 CUT and Tag (Abcam ab8895) in the same lines. Occupancy was confirmed by ER ChIP-qPCR after 3 days of hormone depletion in charcoal/dextran-stripped serum and 24 hours of 10 nmol/L estradiol or ethanol, with the GREB1 promoter as positive control. Function was tested by CRISPR/Cas9 deletion of the approximately 500 bp region using a flanking sgRNA pair (L-sgRNA in px458-GFP, R-sgRNA in pLKO5.sgRNA.EFS.tRFP), giving deletion clones WT_D2 and Y537S_E5 against control clones WT_C10, WT_C11, Y537S_D4 and Y537S_Z99, with a screening PCR product about 700 bp shorter in deleted cells. Phenotypes were CellTiter-Glo at days 0, 3 and 7 (750 cells per well, three biological replicates), collagen I adhesion (100 microgram/mL, 30,000 cells, 30 minutes), crystal violet after 7 days with vehicle, 1 nmol/L estradiol, 100 nmol/L fulvestrant or both, fulvestrant dose response from 1 to 1,000 nmol/L (six biological replicates), long-term 10 nmol/L fulvestrant over 3 weeks with passaging every 3 days (four biological replicates), methylcellulose colony growth (1,000 GFP-positive cells in 1.5% methylcellulose on ultralow attachment plates, imaged 7 days) including an IGFBP3 overexpression rescue arm, and xenografts of 1 x 10^5 MCF7 cells in Matrigel injected into the fourth mammary fat pad of 6 to 8 week old ovariectomized female NSG mice (Jackson strain 005557), measured to 8 weeks. Transcriptional output came from RNA-seq (two biological replicates of each single deletion clone, two control clones per genotype, 15 million paired-end reads, STAR to GRCh37, DESeq2, FDR < 0.05) crossed against a published list of 425 Y537S-specific upregulated genes, plus qRT-PCR validation. Human relevance came from the MET500 metastatic cohort (91 RNA-seq samples from dbGaP phs000673.v2.p1, Salmon and edgeR TMM, 46 ER-positive analyzed, 12 ESR1-mutant versus 34 wild-type). Finally IGFBP3 itself was knocked out with two exon 1 sgRNAs, giving clones B2, E9 and F9 validated by ELISA (Invitrogen EHIGFBP3).

key_methods.name: ERalpha ChIP-seq and cross-dataset peak intersection
key_methods.plain_explanation: Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing finds where a protein sits on DNA across the whole genome. Cells are treated with formaldehyde so proteins are chemically locked onto the DNA they touch, the DNA is broken into short pieces by sonication, an antibody pulls down the pieces attached to the protein of interest (here the estrogen receptor), and those pieces are sequenced. Positions where many more fragments pile up than in a control sample are called peaks and are interpreted as binding sites.
key_methods.how_used: ER ChIP-seq was done in BRx68 cells, two biological replicates each with 10 nmol/L estradiol or ethanol vehicle for 24 hours, with the Santa Cruz HC-20 antibody and IgG and sonicated input as controls. MACS2 v2.2.7.1 called peaks at FDR < 0.05 against input, giving 1,361 peaks in the vehicle condition and 1,864 with estradiol. Peaks were annotated with ChIPseeker (promoter defined as plus or minus 1 kb of the transcription start site) and compared with MCF7 wild-type and Y537S peaks and with three published MCF7 Y537S datasets. For single-replicate datasets, wild-type peaks were simply subtracted with bedtools -v; only the replicated Jeselsohn dataset was analyzed statistically with DESeq2 (log2 fold change > 1, FDR < 0.05).
key_methods.why_it_matters: This is the step that nominated the candidate, so the whole paper rests on it. The caveat is that subtracting wild-type peaks with bedtools is not a statistical test of differential binding, and BRx68 is heterozygous for Y537S, so the immunoprecipitated receptor pool mixes mutant and wild-type ERalpha and peaks cannot be assigned to the mutant allele.

key_methods.name: ATAC-seq and H3K4me1 CUT and Tag for chromatin state
key_methods.plain_explanation: ATAC-seq measures which stretches of DNA are physically accessible. A transposase enzyme called Tn5 cuts and inserts sequencing adapters only where the DNA is not tightly wrapped in nucleosomes, so sequencing the resulting fragments maps open chromatin. CUT and Tag maps a specific histone modification instead: an antibody against the modification is bound inside intact cells, then a Tn5 enzyme fused to protein A/G is recruited to that antibody and tags the nearby DNA. H3K4me1 is a chemical mark on histone H3 that is characteristic of enhancers, which are regulatory DNA segments that boost transcription of genes often far away, as opposed to promoters, which sit at the start of a gene and carry H3K4me3 instead.
key_methods.how_used: ATAC-seq used 50,000 cells per sample with Nextera Tn5 (37 degrees C, 30 minutes) and 10 million paired-end reads, in MCF7 wild-type, Y537S and D538G cells, with differential openness from featureCounts and DESeq2 (log2 fold change > 1, FDR < 0.05). H3K4me1 CUT and Tag used the EpiCypher CUTANA protocol with 25,000 cells per well, concanavalin A beads, 1 microgram of Abcam ab8895 anti-H3K4me1 overnight, a protein A/G-Tn5 fusion, and 10 million paired-end reads. Both were displayed as tracks over the DPY19L1P1 intronic region in Fig. 2B and 2C, alongside cumulative ENCODE H3K4me1, H3K27ac and H3K4me3 from seven cell lines in Fig. 2A.
key_methods.why_it_matters: These data are what justify calling the region an enhancer rather than an incidental ER binding site: strong H3K4me1 and H3K27ac with minimal H3K4me3, open chromatin in all three genotypes but stronger in Y537S. The caveat is that the comparison is shown as genome-browser tracks over one locus, and the figure legend does not report replicate numbers or a statistic for the Y537S versus wild-type openness difference at this specific region.

key_methods.name: ER ChIP-qPCR with the GREB1 promoter as positive control
key_methods.plain_explanation: This is the same immunoprecipitation as ChIP-seq, but instead of sequencing everything, quantitative PCR measures how much DNA from one chosen short region was pulled down. It is a targeted, quantitative confirmation at a single locus and can be run across several conditions cheaply.
key_methods.how_used: MCF7 wild-type and Y537S cells were hormone-depleted for 3 days in charcoal/dextran-stripped serum, then treated 24 hours with 10 nmol/L estradiol or ethanol. Enrichment was measured at the GREB1 promoter (a canonical, well-established estrogen-induced ER target used as the positive control) and at the DPY19L1P1 region (Fig. 2D), with two-way ANOVA and Tukey correction (*** P < 0.001, **** P < 0.0001).
key_methods.why_it_matters: It converts a cross-dataset bioinformatic observation into a direct measurement in isogenic cells, and shows that Y537S ER occupies the region in the absence of hormone more than estrogen-activated wild-type ER does. It also produced the paper's most puzzling result: estradiol significantly decreased Y537S occupancy at this enhancer, the opposite of the GREB1 promoter behavior, which is not explained in the text that could be read.

key_methods.name: CRISPR/Cas9 deletion of a non-coding element with a flanking sgRNA pair
key_methods.plain_explanation: CRISPR/Cas9 is a programmable DNA-cutting system: a short guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to cut at a matching genomic sequence. Using two guide RNAs that flank a region makes two cuts, and the cell religates the ends, deleting the piece in between. This is how a regulatory element that encodes no protein can be removed to ask whether it is functionally required, which is the key distinction from simply observing that a protein binds there.
key_methods.how_used: An L-sgRNA (TGGGACGTTAAGGTGTTGAT, in px458-GFP) and an R-sgRNA (CGTGCAGTTTGGTTCTTCAC, in pLKO5.sgRNA.EFS.tRFP) flanked the roughly 500 bp region. Double-positive single cells were sorted into 96-well plates and screened by PCR (F ACCAGTAGCTGCCAAAGTTTA, R TGAACATCAACATCCAGTCATT), with the deleted allele giving a product about 700 bp shorter. One deletion clone per genotype was taken forward, WT_D2 and Y537S_E5, against control clones WT_C10, WT_C11, Y537S_D4 and Y537S_Z99. A separate IGFBP3 coding knockout used two exon 1 sgRNAs in px458, giving clones B2, E9 and F9 validated by ELISA.
key_methods.why_it_matters: This is the causal core of the paper, and the parallel wild-type deletion is the control that makes the phenotype mutation-specific rather than generically growth-related. The design weakness is that only a single deletion clone per genotype was used, so clone-to-clone variation and CRISPR off-target or passenger effects are not excluded, and there is no re-insertion rescue of the deleted element.

key_methods.name: RNA-seq of deletion clones crossed against mutant-specific gene lists
key_methods.plain_explanation: RNA sequencing counts how many transcripts of each gene a sample contains, so two conditions can be compared to find differentially expressed genes. The usual statistical tool, DESeq2, models the counts and reports a fold change plus a false discovery rate. Here the comparison was filtered against an independently published list of genes already known to be higher in Y537S cells, so that only genes that are both mutant-driven and enhancer-dependent remained.
key_methods.how_used: Two biological replicates of each single deletion clone, against two control clones per genotype, were sequenced at 15 million paired-end reads, aligned with STAR v2.7.9a to GRCh37, counted with featureCounts, and analyzed with DESeq2 v1.30.1 (FDR < 0.05, log2 fold change > 0 for the deletion comparisons, log2 fold change > 1 for mutant versus wild-type). Deletion in Y537S cells changed 503 genes down and 379 up; in wild-type cells 184 down and 336 up; 451 down and 321 up were unique to Y537S. Crossing the Y537S-specific downregulated set with 425 published Y537S-specific upregulated genes left 10 genes, including IGFBP3 (chromosome 7, about 14 Mb from the enhancer) and CD44 (chromosome 11). A vehicle-correction step removed genes significantly higher in wild-type vehicle than wild-type estradiol from the Y537S vehicle versus wild-type estradiol list.
key_methods.why_it_matters: It is what turns an anonymous enhancer into a named mechanism, and the intersection logic is a sensible way to avoid clone-specific noise. The limitation is severe though: the two RNA-seq replicates are two biological replicates of the same single clone, not independent clones, so a clone-specific transcriptional artifact would be indistinguishable from a true enhancer effect.

key_methods.name: Ovariectomized NSG mouse mammary fat pad xenograft
key_methods.plain_explanation: A xenograft is human cancer cells implanted into a mouse. NSG mice lack functional T, B and natural killer cells, so human cells are not rejected. Ovariectomy removes the ovaries and therefore the main source of circulating estrogen, so the mouse is estrogen-deprived. Together this tests whether cells can grow as a tumor without hormone support, which is the in vivo equivalent of the endocrine-deprived clinical setting that selects for ESR1 mutations.
key_methods.how_used: MCF7 cells were hormone-deprived for 3 days, then 1 x 10^5 cells in 100 microliters of PBS with Matrigel were injected into the fourth mammary fat pad of 6 to 8 week old ovariectomized female NSG mice (Jackson strain 005557, USC IACUC #20431). Tumor volume was followed by caliper and tumor weight recorded at 8 weeks (Fig. 3E), with two-way ANOVA and an unpaired t test.
key_methods.why_it_matters: It shows the enhancer requirement is not an artifact of plastic culture: deletion reduced both tumor volume and weight in Y537S cells but not wild-type, and Y537S control tumors were larger than wild-type, consistent with ligand-independent growth. The caveat is that the number of mice per group is not stated in the methods text that could be read, and the immunodeficient, estrogen-free host excludes any immune or stromal estrogen contribution.

key_methods.name: MET500 metastatic cohort reanalysis
key_methods.plain_explanation: MET500 is a public collection of RNA sequencing from metastatic human tumors with linked clinical and mutation data. Reanalyzing it lets a cell-line finding be checked in real patient tumors without new sample collection, by comparing expression of a gene between patients who do and do not carry a mutation of interest.
key_methods.how_used: FASTQ files for 91 metastatic breast cancer samples were downloaded from dbGaP (phs000673.v2.p1), quantified with Salmon v0.8.2, summarized with tximport, TMM normalized in edgeR and converted to log2 counts per million. ESR1 mutation status came from the MET500 portal. Among the 46 ER-positive samples, IGFBP3 was compared between 12 ESR1-mutant and 34 ESR1 wild-type tumors by two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Fig. 4F).
key_methods.why_it_matters: It is the only human tumor evidence in the paper and it makes IGFBP3 more than a cell-line curiosity. The caveats are that n = 12 mutant samples is small, the comparison is cross-sectional rather than causal, bulk RNA cannot separate tumor-cell from stromal IGFBP3, and no correction for testing multiple candidate genes is described.

key_concepts.plain_definition: ESR1 is the human gene that encodes estrogen receptor alpha (ERalpha), a protein that sits mostly in the nucleus, binds the hormone estrogen, and then binds specific DNA sequences to switch nearby genes on or off. It is therefore a hormone-controlled transcription factor. In breast tissue, estrogen acting through ERalpha drives proliferation of the epithelium, and in roughly 80% of breast cancers the tumor cells still express ERalpha and still depend on this signal, which is why drugs that block it work. In this paper ERalpha is both the protein whose DNA binding was mapped and, in mutant form, the driver whose downstream element was hunted.

The ligand-binding domain is the part of ERalpha that forms a pocket for estrogen. When estrogen enters, the domain changes shape, in particular a short helix (helix 12) folds over the pocket, and that new shape is what recruits the coactivator proteins needed to turn genes on. Single amino acid substitutions at a few recurring positions, most often tyrosine 537 changed to serine (Y537S) and aspartate 538 changed to glycine (D538G), stabilize that active shape even with no estrogen present, so the receptor behaves as if permanently hormone-stimulated. The same shape change also lowers the pocket's affinity for antagonist drugs, which is why these mutants resist endocrine therapy. They are found in 18% to 53% of patients whose ER-positive breast cancer progressed on endocrine therapy and are essentially absent before treatment, so they are a classic acquired-resistance mutation. This paper asks what Y537S does to the genome that activated normal ERalpha does not.

An enhancer is a short stretch of DNA, typically a few hundred base pairs, that contains binding sites for transcription factors and increases how much a target gene is transcribed. Unlike a promoter, which sits immediately at the start of a gene, an enhancer can lie tens of thousands or even millions of base pairs away, inside another gene's intron, or on the far side of unrelated genes, and it reaches its target by the DNA looping so that the two come into physical contact. Enhancers are recognized experimentally by a combination of signals: the DNA is accessible (detected by ATAC-seq), the surrounding histones carry H3K4me1 and H3K27ac but little H3K4me3, and transcription factors are bound there. In this paper the candidate element is a 446 bp enhancer inside the first intron of a pseudogene, and the central claim is that deleting it, not just observing binding at it, changes cell behavior.

An ERE is the specific DNA sequence that ERalpha recognizes. The ideal version is a palindrome, two copies of the half-site GGTCA arranged in opposite orientations separated by three spacer bases, which lets two ERalpha molecules bind as a pair, one on each half. Real genomic EREs are often imperfect or reduced to a single half-site, and such weaker sites often depend on neighboring factors to be used. The DPY19L1P1 element contains both a palindromic ERE (AGGTCAcaaaGACCc) and an antisense half-site (caGGTCA), which is the sequence-level reason to believe ERalpha binds there directly rather than being tethered by another protein.

A pseudogene is a stretch of DNA that looks like a gene, because it arose by duplication of a real gene or by reverse transcription of a messenger RNA back into the genome, but has accumulated changes that stop it producing a working protein. Pseudogenes were long treated as genomic debris, yet many of them still contain functional regulatory DNA, and some produce regulatory RNAs. DPY19L1P1 is a pseudogene on chromosome 7 derived from the DPY19L1 family. The point here is that the enhancer is simply located inside its first intron: nothing in the readable text claims the pseudogene itself is transcribed or functional, so DPY19L1P1 should be read as an address, not as a mechanism.

IGFBP3 (insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3) is a secreted protein and the most abundant of the six IGF-binding proteins in blood. Its primary job is to bind the growth factors IGF1 and IGF2 with high affinity, which keeps them in circulation, extends their half-life, and controls how much free growth factor is available to stimulate the IGF1 receptor on cells. Because of this, IGFBP3 can suppress growth by sequestering IGFs away from the receptor, or promote growth by delivering them to it, and it has additional IGF-independent activities inside and on cells. The literature is genuinely two-sided, with reported proapoptotic and reported proproliferative effects (the paper cites refs 51 to 54 for both). In this paper IGFBP3 is the enhancer-dependent, Y537S-specific gene that was validated functionally: knocking it out reduced proliferation, so in this context it behaves as growth-promoting.

The insulin-like growth factor axis is the signaling system built from the ligands IGF1 and IGF2, the receptors they act on (chiefly IGF1R, plus the insulin receptor), and the six IGF-binding proteins including IGFBP3 that control ligand availability. When IGF1 engages IGF1R, the receptor autophosphorylates and turns on the PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways, which drive cell survival, growth and proliferation. The amount of signal a cell actually receives therefore depends not only on how much IGF1 is around but on how it is partitioned among the binding proteins, which is why a change in IGFBP3 is a change in IGF tone rather than a simple on or off. In breast biology the IGF axis cooperates extensively with estrogen signaling, and this paper is relevant precisely because it places an IGF-axis component downstream of an ERalpha-bound enhancer.

key_concepts.term: Endocrine therapy, SERMs, SERDs and aromatase inhibitors
key_concepts.plain_definition: Endocrine therapy is the set of treatments that cut off estrogen signaling in ER-positive breast cancer. Selective estrogen receptor modulators such as tamoxifen compete with estrogen for the ERalpha binding pocket and block its activating effect in breast tissue. Selective estrogen receptor degraders such as fulvestrant (also called ICI182780, abbreviated ICI in this paper) not only block the pocket but cause the receptor protein itself to be destroyed, lowering total ERalpha. Aromatase inhibitors take a different route and block CYP19A1, the aromatase enzyme that converts androgens into estrogens in peripheral tissues, which is the main estrogen source after menopause. This paper uses fulvestrant throughout as the resistance readout, because Y537S cells remain able to grow under it while wild-type cells do not.

Circulating tumor cells are cancer cells that have left a tumor and are travelling in the blood. They are extremely rare, usually a handful per millilitre among billions of blood cells, so capturing them and then expanding them into a stable cell line that grows indefinitely in culture is difficult and uncommon. When it works, the resulting line is a patient-derived model of metastatic, treatment-exposed disease, which is closer to the clinical setting than a decades-old laboratory line. BRx68 is such a line, from a patient with luminal metastatic breast cancer, and it carries ESR1 Y537S on one allele. Its value here is that the mutation arose in a patient rather than being engineered, but the trade-off is that it is a single patient's cells, is heterozygous, and has no isogenic wild-type counterpart.

key_concepts.term: Histone marks H3K4me1, H3K27ac and H3K4me3
key_concepts.plain_definition: DNA in the nucleus is wound around histone proteins, and chemical groups added to the histone tails act as labels that report, and help determine, what the underlying DNA is doing. Three labels matter for identifying regulatory DNA: H3K4me1 (one methyl group on lysine 4 of histone H3) marks enhancers, whether poised or active; H3K27ac (an acetyl group on lysine 27) marks regulatory elements that are actively working; and H3K4me3 (three methyl groups on lysine 4) marks promoters at gene start sites. A region with strong H3K4me1 and H3K27ac but little H3K4me3 is therefore read as an active enhancer rather than a promoter, and that is exactly the pattern reported for the DPY19L1P1 element from ENCODE data across seven cell lines in Fig. 2A.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.title: ERalpha binding landscape in the BRx68 Y537S circulating tumor cell line
figures.question: Does mutant ERalpha in a patient-derived Y537S circulating tumor cell line occupy a different set of genomic sites than estrogen-activated wild-type ERalpha, and are there sites unique to the mutant context?
figures.how_to_read: Panel A is a sample-by-sample similarity heatmap built from the percentage of overlapping significant peaks, so darker or higher values mean two samples share more binding sites; replicates clustering together is the quality check. Panel B is a stacked feature-distribution bar chart assigning every peak to a genomic category (promoter defined as plus or minus 1 kb of the transcription start site, exon, intron, untranslated region, distal intergenic), comparing BRx68 with and without estradiol against doxycycline-inducible MCF7 Y537S with and without estradiol. Panels C and D are binding-intensity heatmaps where each row is one genomic region and the signal is BRx68 ER ChIP-seq: panel C uses significant activated wild-type ER peaks as the reference regions, panel D uses Y537S-unique peaks, with representative Washington Epigenome Browser tracks shown beneath each.
figures.key_result: At FDR < 0.05 versus input, BRx68 had 1,361 ER peaks in vehicle and 1,864 with estradiol. The feature distribution shifted with hormone: promoter-proximal peaks were relatively more common in vehicle and distal intergenic peaks more common with estradiol, whereas MCF7 Y537S showed no obvious vehicle versus estradiol difference. Of the 1,361 vehicle peaks, 753 were shared with both wild-type and Y537S MCF7 peaks, only 124 overlapped Y537S-unique regions, and 484 were unique to BRx68 vehicle (Supplementary Fig. S1A). The legend reports no sample sizes, error bars or statistics for the panels.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.title: A 446 bp region in the first intron of DPY19L1P1 has enhancer features and is preferentially bound by Y537S ERalpha
figures.question: Is the candidate mutant-shared binding site a genuine enhancer, is it more accessible in mutant cells, and does Y537S ERalpha occupy it more than estrogen-activated wild-type ERalpha does?
figures.how_to_read: Panel A is a genome-browser view over the DPY19L1P1 first intron showing bigwig ER ChIP-seq tracks from Jeselsohn and colleagues plus the BRx68 data, aligned under cumulative ENCODE H3K4me1, H3K27ac and H3K4me3 tracks from seven cell lines, so the vertical comparison is binding against chromatin state at the same coordinates. Panels B and C are the same browser window showing ATAC-seq (open chromatin) and H3K4me1 CUT and Tag tracks for MCF7 wild-type, Y537S and D538G cells, so track height is signal and the comparison is between genotypes at one locus. Panel D is ChIP-qPCR bar graphs of ER enrichment, the GREB1 promoter on the left as positive control and the DPY19L1P1 region on the right, in wild-type and Y537S cells with and without estradiol after 3 days of hormone depletion and 24 hours of 10 nmol/L estradiol or ethanol.
figures.key_result: The region is a 446 bp interval in the DPY19L1P1 first intron at chr7:32,720,197 to 32,720,643, with log2 fold change > 2 for mutant versus wild-type ER binding in the Jeselsohn dataset. ENCODE data show strong H3K4me1 and H3K27ac but minimal H3K4me3, the enhancer signature. ATAC-seq shows the region open in wild-type, Y537S and D538G cells with stronger signal in Y537S, and CUT and Tag shows H3K4me1 enrichment in wild-type and Y537S. The region contains a palindromic ERE (AGGTCAcaaaGACCc) plus an antisense half-site (caGGTCA) (Supplementary Fig. S1B). By ChIP-qPCR, Y537S cells showed significantly enriched ER binding at the GREB1 promoter with estradiol, Y537S vehicle showed higher DPY19L1P1 enrichment than activated wild-type, and notably estradiol treatment of Y537S cells significantly decreased DPY19L1P1 enrichment relative to vehicle. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey correction, *** P < 0.001, **** P < 0.0001; no sample sizes or error bar definitions are given in the legend.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.title: Deleting the enhancer impairs proliferation, adhesion, fulvestrant resistance and tumorigenicity in Y537S cells only
figures.question: Is the enhancer functionally required, and is the requirement specific to cells carrying ESR1 Y537S rather than a general growth requirement?
figures.how_to_read: Every panel runs the deletion clone against control clones in parallel in two genotypes, wild-type and Y537S, so the mutation specificity is read by comparing the two genotype blocks rather than by any single bar. Panel A plots CellTiter-Glo luminescence (a proxy for viable cell number) at days 0, 3 and 7 in full serum. Panel B is crystal violet absorbance after a 30 minute collagen I adhesion assay, in full media on top and hormone-stripped serum below. Panel C is 7 day crystal violet growth in stripped serum under four conditions (vehicle, 1 nmol/L estradiol, 100 nmol/L fulvestrant, estradiol plus fulvestrant), normalized to vehicle. Panel D is fold change from initial seeding after 3 weeks of 10 nmol/L fulvestrant with passaging every 3 days. Panel E is xenograft tumor volume over time and tumor weight at 8 weeks after mammary fat pad injection into ovariectomized mice.
figures.key_result: Y537S deletion cells grew less than Y537S controls at days 3 and 7, with no difference in wild-type (panel A, two-way ANOVA with Tukey). Collagen adhesion was reduced in Y537S deletion cells in both full and stripped media but not in wild-type (panel B, one-way ANOVA with Tukey). Under fulvestrant, Y537S deletion cells were reduced with fulvestrant alone and with estradiol plus fulvestrant but wild-type was not (panel C, two-way ANOVA with Sidak), and in the dose response (Supplementary Fig. S2B) Y537S deletion cells were more sensitive at 10 and 100 nmol/L fulvestrant without estradiol while wild-type showed no difference. Over 3 weeks of 10 nmol/L fulvestrant, wild-type cells grew to under 10% of vehicle, Y537S controls to about 50%, and Y537S deletion cells were significantly lower than Y537S controls (panel D, described as a Mann-Whitney unpaired t test). In vivo at 8 weeks, Y537S deletion reduced both tumor volume and tumor weight while wild-type was unchanged, and Y537S control tumors were larger than wild-type (panel E, two-way ANOVA and unpaired t test). Group sizes for the xenograft are not stated.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.title: RNA-seq of deletion clones identifies IGFBP3 and CD44 as Y537S-specific enhancer-dependent genes
figures.question: Which genes does this enhancer actually control in mutant cells, and is any of them also elevated in ESR1-mutant human tumors?
figures.how_to_read: Panel A is a Venn diagram of differentially expressed genes from the deletion versus control comparison within each genotype (log2 fold change > 0, FDR < 0.05), so the non-overlapping sectors are the genotype-specific responses. Panel B is a second Venn intersecting genes upregulated in Y537S vehicle versus wild-type estradiol (that is, mutant-specific genes) with genes downregulated after deletion in Y537S cells, so the overlap is the shortlist of mutant-driven, enhancer-dependent genes. Panels C to E are qRT-PCR bar charts for IGFBP3 and CD44 normalized to 36B4, panel C in full media (one-way ANOVA with Dunnett), panels D and E in stripped serum after 24 hours of vehicle, 1 nmol/L estradiol, 10 nmol/L fulvestrant or estradiol plus fulvestrant (two-way ANOVA with Tukey). Panel F is a boxplot of IGFBP3 expression in MET500 ER-positive metastases split by ESR1 mutation status.
figures.key_result: Deletion changed 503 genes down and 379 up in Y537S cells versus 184 down and 336 up in wild-type, with 451 down and 321 up unique to Y537S. Intersecting with 425 previously reported Y537S-specific upregulated genes left 10 genes also downregulated only in Y537S deletion cells, including IGFBP3 (chromosome 7, about 14 Mb from the enhancer) and CD44 (chromosome 11). qRT-PCR confirmed both in stripped serum (Supplementary Fig. S3A) and full media (panel C). Under fulvestrant, IGFBP3 remained lower in Y537S deletion cells than controls (panel D), whereas CD44 was lower mainly with estradiol (panel E), which is why the authors favor IGFBP3 as the downstream target; GREB1 served as the positive control (Supplementary Fig. S3B). In MET500, IGFBP3 was significantly higher in ESR1-mutant (n = 12) than wild-type (n = 34) ER-positive metastases by two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test (panel F). * P < 0.05, **** P < 0.0001.

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.title: IGFBP3 knockout reduces proliferation but does not restore fulvestrant sensitivity
figures.question: Is IGFBP3 itself functionally responsible for the enhancer-dependent phenotypes, and can restoring IGFBP3 rescue the deletion?
figures.how_to_read: Panel A is an IGFBP3 ELISA on conditioned medium, validating loss of secreted protein across wild-type control, wild-type deletion, Y537S control, Y537S deletion and the three Y537S IGFBP3 knockout clones (B2, E9, F9) plus a control sgRNA clone. Panel B is CellTiter-Glo at days 0 and 7 in full media for IGFBP3 knockout versus control Y537S cells (two-way ANOVA with Dunnett). Panel C is CellTiter-Glo in stripped serum after 7 days with vehicle or 10 or 100 nmol/L fulvestrant without estradiol (two-way ANOVA with Tukey). Panel D is methylcellulose colony growth relative to day 1 in suspension for wild-type control, wild-type deletion, Y537S control and Y537S deletion cells, each carrying either empty control plasmid or an IGFBP3 overexpression construct, so the paired bars within each genotype are the rescue test (Welch's t test).
figures.key_result: All three IGFBP3 knockout clones lost detectable secreted IGFBP3 by ELISA (panel A). Two of the three clones had significantly reduced proliferation at day 7 and the third did not (panel B). IGFBP3 loss did not significantly change fulvestrant sensitivity (panel C). In the methylcellulose assay (panel D), Y537S control cells formed colonies better than wild-type controls, enhancer deletion did not significantly change wild-type growth, and enhancer deletion suppressed Y537S colony growth. The outcome of the IGFBP3 overexpression rescue arm could not be read: the available full text is truncated mid-sentence in this paragraph, at the words 'whereas o'. No sample sizes or error bar definitions are given in the legend.

key_findings.statement: A 446 bp region in the first intron of the pseudogene DPY19L1P1 at chr7:32,720,197 to 32,720,643 carries an active enhancer signature and is occupied by ESR1 Y537S ERalpha in the absence of hormone more than by estrogen-activated wild-type ERalpha.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 2A shows ER ChIP-seq bigwigs over the locus under cumulative ENCODE tracks with strong H3K4me1 and H3K27ac but minimal H3K4me3, and log2 fold change > 2 for mutant versus wild-type in the Jeselsohn dataset. Fig. 2B shows ATAC-seq openness in wild-type, Y537S and D538G cells, stronger in Y537S. Fig. 2C shows H3K4me1 by CUT and Tag. Fig. 2D ChIP-qPCR shows higher enrichment in Y537S vehicle than activated wild-type, with the GREB1 promoter as positive control, two-way ANOVA with Tukey. Supplementary Fig. S1B reports a palindromic ERE (AGGTCAcaaaGACCc) and an antisense half-site. Table 1 lists it among regions shared across three published mutant ER datasets.

key_findings.statement: CRISPR deletion of this enhancer impairs proliferation, collagen adhesion, anchorage-independent colony growth and mammary fat pad tumor growth specifically in ESR1 Y537S cells, with no comparable effect in isogenic wild-type cells.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 3A (CellTiter-Glo days 3 and 7), Fig. 3B (collagen adhesion in full and stripped media), Fig. 3E (reduced tumor volume and weight at 8 weeks in ovariectomized NSG mice, with Y537S control tumors larger than wild-type), Fig. 5D (methylcellulose colony growth suppressed in Y537S deletion but not wild-type deletion). The parallel wild-type deletion clone WT_D2 is the specificity control in every panel.

key_findings.statement: Loss of the enhancer re-sensitizes Y537S cells to fulvestrant, so the element contributes to endocrine resistance and not only to growth.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 3C (7 day crystal violet in stripped serum, reduced with 100 nmol/L fulvestrant alone and with estradiol plus fulvestrant in Y537S only, two-way ANOVA with Sidak), Fig. 3D (after 3 weeks of 10 nmol/L fulvestrant, wild-type grew to under 10% of vehicle, Y537S controls to about 50%, Y537S deletion significantly lower than Y537S controls), Supplementary Fig. S2B (increased sensitivity at 10 and 100 nmol/L fulvestrant without estradiol, wild-type unaffected).

key_findings.statement: IGFBP3 is a Y537S-specific, enhancer-dependent gene, selected from a 10 gene shortlist and favored over CD44 because its reduction persists under fulvestrant.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 4A and 4B Venn diagrams (503 down and 379 up after deletion in Y537S versus 184 down and 336 up in wild-type; 451 down and 321 up unique to Y537S; 10 of 425 published Y537S-specific upregulated genes also downregulated only in Y537S deletion cells, including IGFBP3 on chromosome 7 about 14 Mb away and CD44 on chromosome 11). Fig. 4C qRT-PCR in full media and Supplementary Fig. S3A in stripped serum. Fig. 4D shows IGFBP3 stays lower in deletion cells under fulvestrant, whereas Fig. 4E shows CD44 differs mainly with estradiol.

key_findings.statement: IGFBP3 is functionally required for part of the growth phenotype but not for fulvestrant resistance, so the enhancer must act on resistance through additional genes.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 5A ELISA confirms loss of secreted IGFBP3 in clones B2, E9 and F9. Fig. 5B shows significantly reduced day 7 proliferation in two of three clones, with the third not significant (two-way ANOVA with Dunnett). Fig. 5C shows no significant change in fulvestrant sensitivity at 10 or 100 nmol/L without estradiol.

key_findings.statement: IGFBP3 expression is higher in ESR1-mutant than ESR1 wild-type ER-positive human metastases, which supports clinical relevance of the mutant-to-IGFBP3 link.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 4F boxplot of the MET500 cohort, 12 ESR1-mutant versus 34 wild-type among the 46 ER-positive samples of 91 total, two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

key_findings.statement: ER binding in the patient-derived BRx68 Y537S circulating tumor cell line is largely distinct from MCF7 ER binding, and most BRx68 peaks do not fall in previously defined Y537S-unique regions, which is why cross-dataset intersection rather than BRx68 alone was needed to nominate the enhancer.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 1A replicate clustering, Fig. 1B feature distribution (promoter-proximal peaks relatively more common in vehicle, distal intergenic with estradiol, no equivalent shift in MCF7 Y537S), Fig. 1C and 1D heatmaps, and Supplementary Fig. S1A: of 1,361 BRx68 vehicle peaks, 753 shared with wild-type and Y537S MCF7, only 124 overlapping Y537S-unique regions, and 484 unique to BRx68.

key_findings.statement: Estradiol reduces rather than increases Y537S ERalpha occupancy at this enhancer, which distinguishes it from a conventional estrogen-induced element such as the GREB1 promoter.
key_findings.evidence: Fig. 2D right panel: estradiol treatment of Y537S cells significantly decreased DPY19L1P1 enrichment compared with vehicle, while the same cells showed significantly increased binding at the GREB1 promoter with estradiol. Consistent with Fig. 3C and Supplementary Fig. S2B, where the deletion phenotype under fulvestrant was clearest in the absence of estradiol.

limitations: The Discussion section could not be read. The Europe PMC full-text deposit for PMC13662453 is truncated mid-sentence inside the Results subsection on IGFBP3 knockout, at the words 'whereas o' in the methylcellulose paragraph, and the PubTator3 BioC export returned client errors on three attempts. The authors' own stated caveats, the data availability statement and sequencing accession numbers, and the outcome of the IGFBP3 overexpression rescue arm shown in Fig. 5D were therefore unavailable and are not represented in this analysis.

The functional core rests on a single deletion clone per genotype, WT_D2 and Y537S_E5. Worse, the RNA-seq 'two biological replicates' are two replicates of that same single clone, with two independent control clones per genotype. This is an asymmetric design in which a clone-specific transcriptional or growth artifact, or a CRISPR off-target or passenger event, cannot be distinguished from a genuine enhancer effect. Independent deletion clones are the missing control.

Deleting roughly 500 bp of genomic DNA removes every feature it contains, not only the ER binding site. There is no orthogonal perturbation that leaves the sequence intact, such as CRISPRi silencing, dCas9 tethering, ERE point mutation, or re-insertion rescue of the element, so the paper shows the interval is required but not that ER binding to the ERE is the operative mechanism.

The enhancer-to-IGFBP3 assignment is inferred from co-regulation and genomic neighbourhood, not demonstrated. IGFBP3 lies about 14 Mb from the element on chromosome 7, which is far beyond a typical topologically associating domain, and no chromatin contact data (Hi-C, 4C, HiChIP or promoter capture) are presented to show the two ever touch. Several of the other nine shortlisted genes, and CD44 on a different chromosome entirely, face the same problem.

Discovery ChIP-seq comes from one patient-derived line, BRx68, with two biological replicates and no isogenic mutation-corrected counterpart. Because Y537S is heterozygous in BRx68, the immunoprecipitated receptor pool mixes mutant and wild-type ERalpha and no peak can be assigned to the mutant allele. For the single-replicate published datasets, wild-type peaks were removed by bedtools subtraction rather than by a statistical test of differential binding, which inflates apparent mutant specificity; only the Jeselsohn dataset was analyzed with DESeq2.

Only 124 of 1,361 BRx68 vehicle peaks overlapped previously defined Y537S-unique regions, so the patient-derived line and the engineered MCF7 lines agree poorly. The enhancer survived as a candidate because of intersection across datasets, which is a reasonable strategy but means the element was selected for cross-model reproducibility rather than for effect size in any one model.

All deletion phenotyping is in MCF7. T47D wild-type and Y537S lines are listed in the Methods but no enhancer deletion in T47D or in BRx68 itself is reported in the readable text, so the mutation-specific requirement has not been shown in a second cellular background, and the D538G line was used only for ATAC and CUT and Tag tracks, never for occupancy or function.

Xenograft group sizes are not stated in the Methods text that could be read, which makes the in vivo result in Fig. 3E hard to weigh. The model is also ovariectomized NSG, that is both estrogen-free and lacking T, B and natural killer cells, so it isolates ligand-independent growth but excludes any immune or host stromal contribution.

The human validation is thin and correlational: 12 ESR1-mutant versus 34 wild-type ER-positive MET500 metastases, cross-sectional, bulk RNA that cannot separate tumor-cell from stromal IGFBP3, with no reported correction for having screened multiple candidate genes, and no test of whether IGFBP3 levels track the enhancer's chromatin state in those tumors.

The causal chain is incomplete and the paper says so by its own data: IGFBP3 knockout reproduced part of the proliferation defect but not the fulvestrant sensitization, so whatever the enhancer does to confer resistance is unaccounted for. Calling IGFBP3 'the' downstream target overstates what Fig. 5 supports.

Estradiol decreased Y537S ER occupancy at the element (Fig. 2D), the opposite of classic estrogen-driven enhancer behavior, and no mechanism for this is offered in the readable text. Since the fulvestrant phenotypes were clearest without estradiol, the hormonal logic of the element is unresolved.

Figure legends do not report sample sizes or error bar definitions for Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4 or Fig. 5, so replicate structure has to be reconstructed from the Methods. The statistical treatment is also loose in places: Fig. 3D is described as a 'Mann-Whitney unpaired t test', which conflates two different tests.

The source contains internal inconsistencies that were not reconciled: the screening-primer product difference is given as 300 bp in the Methods and 200 bp in the Results, and the IGFBP3 sgRNAs are named Sg1.1 and Sg2.1 in the Methods but 1.1 and 3.2 in the Fig. 5 legend.

Genome build is a practical hazard for reuse. RNA-seq was aligned to GRCh37 and the enhancer coordinates chr7:32,720,197 to 32,720,643 are almost certainly GRCh37, but the build is not stated alongside the coordinates, so anyone reusing them must verify before lifting over.

Nothing in the readable text establishes that the DPY19L1P1 pseudogene is itself transcribed or functional, yet naming the enhancer after it invites the reading that the pseudogene matters. The element should be treated as a chromosome 7 interval that happens to lie in that intron.
open_questions: Does the element physically contact the IGFBP3 promoter 14 Mb away, and if so through what looping architecture? Hi-C, 4C from the enhancer, or promoter-capture HiChIP in Y537S versus wild-type cells would settle whether the regulatory link is direct or indirect.

Does IGFBP3 overexpression rescue anchorage-independent colony growth in Y537S enhancer-deleted cells? This arm exists in Fig. 5D but its result sentence falls inside the truncated portion of the available full text, so the strength of the IGFBP3 claim cannot be judged from what was readable.
Which gene or genes among the other nine shortlisted Y537S-specific, enhancer-dependent genes carry the fulvestrant resistance phenotype, given that IGFBP3 knockout did not affect it?

Why does estradiol reduce Y537S ER occupancy at this enhancer while increasing it at the GREB1 promoter? Does the unliganded mutant receptor recruit a different cofactor complex at this element, and is that complex druggable?

Is secreted IGFBP3 acting on these cells through the IGF axis, by changing how much free IGF1 or IGF2 reaches IGF1R, or through IGF-independent activities? The ELISA protocol included a 24 hour insulin incubation before assay, which hints the authors were thinking about ligand availability, but the readable text does not explain it.

Is the enhancer required in D538G cells as well as Y537S? D538G appears only in the ATAC and CUT and Tag tracks, so whether this is a general property of ligand-binding-domain mutants or specific to Y537S is untested.

Does the element have any role in treatment-naive ER-positive tumors, or does it only become load-bearing once an ESR1 mutation appears? The wild-type deletion clone showed no phenotype in culture, which argues for the latter, but was not tested in vivo under estrogen.
reading.relevance_to_lab: The strongest and most actionable connection is to the lab's IGF1 and IGF1R program. This paper places IGFBP3, a core component of the IGF axis, downstream of an ERalpha-occupied enhancer, and validates it functionally (Fig. 4C to 4F, Fig. 5A and 5B). That is a concrete, published precedent for the exact kind of claim the lab's Chen, Han et al. 2026 preprint leaves open, namely whether an IGF-axis gene is a direct ERalpha target downstream of estrogen signaling. It is important to be precise about the mismatch though: the ERalpha here is epithelial, mutant and ligand-independent in a metastatic ER-positive breast cancer cell, not wild-type stromal ERalpha in fallopian tube, and the gene is IGFBP3, not IGF1. So this paper does not answer the lab's question and should not be cited as if it did. What it does provide is a validated workflow the lab can copy directly onto its own question: take estrogen-responsive or condition-specific ER peaks, intersect across independent datasets to drop single-model noise, confirm enhancer identity with ATAC plus H3K4me1 and absence of H3K4me3, confirm occupancy by ChIP-qPCR against a GREB1 promoter positive control, then delete the element with a flanking sgRNA pair and read out the candidate target. Applied to the lab's system, that is the test for whether a stromal-ERalpha-bound enhancer is required for Igf1 expression in fallopian tube fibroblasts. Specific items worth borrowing. First, the enhancer coordinates chr7:32,720,197 to 32,720,643, a 446 bp interval, together with the palindromic ERE AGGTCAcaaaGACCc and the antisense half-site caGGTCA. The motif is immediately usable: scan it against the lab's fallopian tube and mammary ATAC and ER ChIP data to ask whether similar composite ERE configurations sit near IGF1, IGF1R or IGFBP family genes. Note that the build is not stated next to the coordinates and RNA-seq used GRCh37, so confirm before lifting over, and note that the human coordinates do not transfer to the lab's mouse models without orthology work on a pseudogene locus that may have no mouse counterpart. Second, the chromatin resources: MCF7 wild-type, Y537S and D538G ATAC-seq and H3K4me1 CUT and Tag, and the BRx68 ER ChIP-seq. These are ER-positive breast epithelial references the lab can use as comparators for its own ER cistrome work, though accession numbers could not be read because the data availability statement falls in the truncated portion of the deposit and will need to be pulled from the publisher version. Third, IGFBP3 as a readout, which is the cheapest immediate follow-up. The lab should score IGFBP3 in its existing Igf1r knockout RNA-seq dataset: if IGFBP3 moves with Igf1r loss in mammary gland, that positions it inside the lab's own axis rather than as an isolated breast cancer observation, and the direction of change is informative either way. In parallel, score IGFBP3 in the fallopian tube stromal ERalpha datasets, split by compartment, to ask whether stromal estrogen signaling changes epithelial or stromal IGFBP3. IGFBP3 is also attractive mechanistically for the lab's stroma-to-epithelium model because it is secreted, so it fits alongside POSTN, FGF1 and FGF2 as a candidate stromal mediator, and because it is directly measurable in co-culture and organoid conditioned medium by the same commercial ELISA used here (Invitrogen EHIGFBP3). One important caution for interpretation: IGFBP3 is genuinely bidirectional in the literature, reported as both proapoptotic and proproliferative (the paper cites refs 51 to 54), and in this paper knockout reduced proliferation, so IGFBP3 behaves as growth-promoting in Y537S MCF7 cells. The lab must establish direction of effect in its own system rather than importing it. Secondarily, CD44 is the other shortlisted target (Fig. 4B, 4C, 4E) and was estradiol-responsive, which connects to the lab's interest in luminal progenitor and progenitor-like epithelial states, since CD44 is a widely used progenitor and stem-cell marker. Finally, the mouse model is a useful methodological complement to the lab's estrogen-excess fallopian tube work: ovariectomized NSG hosts show what mutant ER can do with no ligand at all, which is the mirror image of asking what excess estrogen does to wild-type stroma. The paper neither supports nor challenges the lab's BRCA1 immune-evasion model and has no bearing on cGAS-STING, NK surveillance or MHC class I, and because the host is immunodeficient it could not have.
discussion_questions: The enhancer sits about 14 Mb from IGFBP3 with no contact data presented, which is far outside a typical topologically associating domain. What evidence would we require before believing a link at that distance, and could we run the same test (4C from the element, or CRISPRi rather than deletion) for a candidate stromal ERalpha enhancer near Igf1 in our fallopian tube system?

Estradiol decreased Y537S ER occupancy at this element while increasing occupancy at the GREB1 promoter (Fig. 2D). What model accounts for ligand-independent binding that ligand actively disrupts, and does it imply a distinct cofactor complex we should be looking for in our own stromal ERalpha ChIP, where we have been assuming conventional estrogen-induced recruitment?

IGFBP3 knockout reproduced part of the proliferation defect but none of the fulvestrant sensitization (Fig. 5B versus 5C). Should we read IGFBP3 as a growth mediator only, and is it worth testing any of the other nine shortlisted genes ourselves, or is the resistance arm simply unexplained in this paper?

If we score IGFBP3 in our Igf1r knockout RNA-seq, what direction do we actually predict, and what would each outcome mean? Specifically, would IGFBP3 behave as an IGF1R-dependent gene, an ERalpha target, or both in mammary gland, and does the bidirectional IGFBP3 literature make the readout uninterpretable without a functional follow-up?

The functional claims rest on one deletion clone per genotype, with RNA-seq replicates being two replicates of that same clone against two independent control clones. What is the minimum clone number and control design we would demand before believing a non-coding deletion phenotype in our own hands, and does that standard change how much weight we give Fig. 3 and Fig. 5?

nodes.label: Do ESR1 mutants act through mutant-specific enhancers?

nodes.label: ESR1 LBD mutations in 18% to 53% of progressing tumors
nodes.detail: About 80% of breast cancers express ERalpha; 30% are innately endocrine resistant and 40% of responders acquire resistance. Y537S and D538G make ERalpha constitutively active and lower antagonist affinity.

nodes.detail: Prior studies (refs 17 to 20) showed mutant ER has distinct transcriptomes and binding landscapes versus activated wild-type ER, but no mutant-unique binding site had been deleted and tested for requirement.

nodes.label: A mutant-bound enhancer is required for Y537S phenotypes
nodes.detail: If mutant-specific ER binding is functional, deleting a mutant-enriched enhancer should impair growth and endocrine resistance in Y537S cells but not in wild-type cells.

entities.description: Estrogen-deprived, immunodeficient in vivo model (1 x 10^5 MCF7 cells, fourth mammary fat pad, 8 weeks) used to test whether the enhancer is required for tumor growth without hormone.

relations.evidence: ERalpha encoded by ESR1 is the transcription factor that executes the estrogen receptor signaling program.
Y537S is a hotspot substitution in the ESR1 ligand-binding domain.
D538G is the other common ESR1 ligand-binding-domain hotspot substitution.
Y537S stabilizes the active ERalpha conformation so the receptor behaves as ligand-activated without estrogen.
ESR1 ligand-binding-domain mutations are found in 18% to 53% of patients progressing on endocrine therapy and show reduced antagonist affinity in modeling and reduced fulvestrant effect in cells.
About 80% of breast cancers express ERalpha, defining the ER-positive disease class.
BRx68 is a patient-derived circulating tumor cell line carrying a heterozygous ESR1 Y537S mutation.
Genetically edited MCF7 Y537S cells were obtained from the Ben Ho Park lab and used throughout as the isogenic mutant model.
The 446 bp element lies in the first intron of the DPY19L1P1 pseudogene at chr7:32,720,197 to 32,720,643.
The element contains a palindromic ERE (AGGTCAcaaaGACCc) and an antisense half-site (caGGTCA).

ER ChIP-qPCR showed higher occupancy in Y537S vehicle cells than in estradiol-activated wild-type cells, and the region showed log2 fold change > 2 for mutant versus wild-type binding in the Jeselsohn dataset.
Strong H3K4me1 across seven ENCODE cell lines and H3K4me1 CUT and Tag signal in wild-type and Y537S MCF7 cells at the element.
Strong H3K27ac with minimal H3K4me3 in cumulative ENCODE data, the pattern expected for an active enhancer rather than a promoter.
ATAC-seq tracks show the element open in wild-type, Y537S and D538G MCF7 cells, with stronger signal in Y537S.
H3K4me1 at the element was mapped by CUTANA CUT and Tag with Abcam ab8895 in MCF7 wild-type, Y537S and D538G cells.
ERalpha ChIP-seq in BRx68 with and without estradiol gave 1,361 and 1,864 peaks at FDR < 0.05 and was intersected with three published MCF7 Y537S datasets.
A flanking sgRNA pair deleted roughly 500 bp of the element, giving clones WT_D2 and Y537S_E5 screened by a PCR product about 700 bp shorter.
Estradiol at 1 or 10 nmol/L was used to activate wild-type ERalpha as the comparator for ligand-independent mutant activity.
Estradiol treatment of Y537S cells significantly decreased ER enrichment at the element compared with vehicle, the opposite of its effect at the GREB1 promoter.
Fulvestrant is a selective estrogen receptor degrader that blocks the ligand pocket and promotes ERalpha degradation.
Aromatase (CYP19A1) converts androgens to estrogens in peripheral tissues and is the target of aromatase inhibitors in postmenopausal patients.
GREB1 served as the canonical estrogen-induced ER target control for ChIP-qPCR enrichment and qRT-PCR hormone responsiveness.
IGFBP3 was downregulated after enhancer deletion in Y537S cells only, confirmed by qRT-PCR in full and hormone-stripped media and persisting under fulvestrant.
CD44 was among the 10 genes both Y537S-specific and downregulated after enhancer deletion, though its reduction was most apparent with estradiol.
Deletion reduced CellTiter-Glo signal at days 3 and 7 in Y537S cells but not wild-type cells.
Deletion reduced collagen I adhesion in Y537S cells in both full and hormone-stripped media, with no effect in wild-type cells.
Deletion increased fulvestrant sensitivity at 10 and 100 nmol/L and lowered 3 week growth under 10 nmol/L fulvestrant relative to Y537S controls, which reached about 50% of vehicle.
Deletion reduced tumor volume and tumor weight at 8 weeks in Y537S cells only; Y537S control tumors were larger than wild-type.
Deletion suppressed methylcellulose colony growth in Y537S cells with no significant change in wild-type cells.
Tumor volume by caliper and tumor weight at 8 weeks after injecting 1 x 10^5 cells into the fourth mammary fat pad of ovariectomized NSG mice.
IGFBP3 is the most abundant IGF-binding protein and controls how much free IGF1 and IGF2 can reach IGF1R.
CRISPR knockout of IGFBP3 (clones B2, E9, F9, validated by ELISA) significantly reduced day 7 proliferation in two of three clones.
IGFBP3 was significantly higher in ESR1-mutant (n = 12) than wild-type (n = 34) ER-positive MET500 metastases by two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
IGFBP3 expression was quantified from MET500 RNA-seq with Salmon and edgeR TMM normalization across the 46 ER-positive samples.
The MET500 samples analyzed are ER-positive metastatic breast cancers.
The element is also accessible by ATAC-seq and carries H3K4me1 in engineered D538G MCF7 cells, but ER occupancy and deletion phenotypes were not tested in D538G.
CD44 is used in the field as a progenitor and stem-cell surface marker in breast cancer, and is reported here as a Y537S-specific enhancer-dependent gene.
The paper links mutant ER to the IGF axis by identifying IGFBP3 as the validated enhancer-dependent target in ER-positive breast cancer cells.
Y537S control cells formed methylcellulose colonies better than wild-type control cells.
